utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On our agenda this mourning is the delivery of the decision under Rule 98 bis, and there a few procedural matters not very important, but with which I would like to deal with after I have read the decision. The Chamber will now deliver its decision under Rule 98 bis. The Chamber has heard oral submissions from the Defence and the Prosecution on the 19th through the 25th of March, 2009. And in reaching its decision the Chamber has considered all of the parties submissions. The Chamber will first give a brief summary of these submissions. The Defence for all three accused requested a judgement of acquittal on all counts of the indictment. The Gotovina Defence submitted that in relation to persecution under Count 1, there is no evidence of an unlawful and discriminatory attack directed against the Serb civilian population, including through Operation Storm. It further submitted that Counts 1 through 3, must be dismissed because the Prosecution has not shown that the shelling that took place, whether unlawful or not, was in fact the cause of the flight of civilians. The Gotovina Defence also submitted that Counts 4 through 9 must be dismissed because no evidence has been presented that Mr. Gotovina had the intent to commit crimes against humanity or war crimes through murder, inhumane acts, destruction or pillage of property or that he made a significant contribution to the commission of such crimes. It added that there is no direct or circumstantial evidence to support the Prosecution's theory of a joint criminal enterprise. In relation to liability, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute, the Gotovina Defence argued that there is no evidence to support the Prosecution's theory that Gotovina failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish crimes committed by his subordinates. The Gotovina Defence further submitted that the Chamber should not be barred from dismissing parts of a count, even where it found that the count would otherwise stand. The Cermak Defence asserted that Mr. Cermak had had no operational function as a part of any Croatian military structures, nor an operational role in relation to the civilian police, that he lacked de facto effective control over any such structures and that the Prosecution had presented no evidence to counter these assertions. The Cermak Defence also asserted that Mr. Cermak's authority to discipline members of the Croatian military was limited to his own subordinates, of whom there were very few, and that there was no evidence that they had committed any crimes charged in the indictment. The Cermak Defence therefore submitted that Mr. Cermak could not be held responsible under any theory of command responsibility. The Cermak Defence further submitted that the evidence failed to demonstrate beyond a reasonable doubt the existence of a joint criminal enterprise and adopted the submissions of the Gotovina Defence in this respect; arguing that the evidence also allowed for a reasonable inference of acts of revenge by the civilian population, individual military personnel, and, perhaps, military personnel grouped together. Based on these submissions, the Cermak Defence argued that the evidence raised a reasonable doubt as to whether there existed any joint criminal enterprise in which Mr. Cermak had participated. The Markac Defence argued, in relation to Count 1, that there is no evidence that Mr. Markac held a discriminatory intent towards the Serb civilian population based on their ethnicity. In relation to Counts 2 and 3, it argued that there is no evidence to sustain the allegation that the civilian population fled due to unlawful shelling or any other unlawful acts carried out by the special police. The Markac Defence further submitted that there is no evidence that Mr. Markac participated in a joint criminal enterprise with the objective of permanently removing the Serb population from Krajina by launching large-scale indiscriminate artillery attacks or by any other means. Finally, the Markac Defence submitted that there is no evidence that Mr. Markac had any ability to prevent, investigate, or prosecute crimes. The Prosecution submitted that it had presented sufficient evidence for every count and every mode of liability alleged in the indictment. The Prosecution stated, in particular, that the evidence showed that the Croatian leadership, including President Tudjman, wanted Serbs to leave Croatia and that it undertook a variety of steps to ensure that they did leave and that they would not return. These steps included unlawful attacks and the creation of a hostile environment for any remaining Serbs in Krajina through, inter alia, widespread and systematic destruction of property, plunder, harassment, intimidation, and murder by Croatian forces, including the special police. The Prosecution submitted that each of the accused significantly contributed to the achievement of the objective of the permanent removal of Serbs from Krajina and that they shared this objective. The Prosecution also submitted that each of the three accused had effective control over one or more of either the Croatian armed forces, the civilian police, or the special police, operating in the indictment area during the indictment period; that each accused knew about crimes committed by members of the units; and that each failed to prevent these members' criminal conduct, or to punish them for that conduct. Rule 98 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides as follows. I quote: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." Under the case law of the Tribunal, the Chamber must examine whether there is evidence upon which a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused. Thus, if a reasonable chamber could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of an accused on the basis of the evidence adduced to a count, then the count must stand. There must be sufficient evidence for each element of an alleged crime and mode of liability. The test would not be satisfied if there were no evidence or if no reasonable chamber could believe the evidence presented. At this stage, the evidence should be taken at its highest for the Prosecution. The Chamber should not take into consideration the credibility and liability of a witness, except if no reasonable chamber could find him or her credible or reliable. As for the applicable law, the Gotovina Defence claimed that the amended Rule 98 bis cannot be operative due to Rule 6(D) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the fact that the case against Mr. Gotovina has been pending since his indictment was confirmed in 2001. The Chamber recalls that Rule 98 bis was amended in December 2004 and that the trial against Mr. Gotovina started in March 2008. Furthermore, Mr. Gotovina was only apprehended in December 2005. Rule 98 bis is a procedural rule and a corollary of the right of an accused to be presumed innocent until proved guilty. In domestic legal systems there are varies procedural avenues which give effect to this right, and they are not necessarily limited to the stage of the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. Limiting the scope of Rule 98 bis decisions was intended to streamline the proceedings in the interests of judicial economy by changing the proceedings from a written to an oral one, and focussing on the counts rather than on the individual charges in an indictment. The rules amendment, excluding acquittals on individual charges, does not prejudice the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty. Effect will ultimately be given to this right in the final written judgement. The Chamber further notes that the failure of the Prosecution to adduce evidence on individual charges has an effect on the proceedings that will, in any event, follow. For the purpose of preparing and presenting its evidence, the Defence will, in effect, be left with no case to answer, in relation to those individual charges. The Chamber will now provide a summary of the indictment. The indictment against Ante Gotovina, Ivan Cermak, and Mladen Markac covers nine counts of crimes allegedly committed from at least July 1995 to 30 September 1995, in the following municipalities of the Krajina area of Croatia: Benkovac, Civljane, Donji Lapac, Drnis, Ervenik, Gracac, Kistanje, Knin, Lisane, Ostrovicke, Lisicic, Nadvode, Obrovac, Oklaj, and Orlic. The indictment period includes Operation Storm, which allegedly lasted from the 4th to the 7th of August, 1995, during which Croatian forces took control of the southern part of Krajina. According to the indictment, at the time, Mr. Gotovina was the commander of the Split Military District of the Croatian army and the overall operational commander of Operation Storm. Mr. Cermak was appointed commander of the Knin garrison on the 5th of August, 1995, and remained in that position throughout the indictment period. Mr. Markac was the commander of the special police, members of which were involved in Operation Storm and in ensuing operations and actions. The first three counts of the document charge persecutions, deportation, and forcible transfer as crimes against humanity. The fourth and fifth counts charge the war crimes of plunder and destruction of property. Counts 6 and 7 charge murder as a crime against humanity and as a war crime. The two final counts charge the crime against humanity of inhumane acts and the war crime of cruel treatment. The indictment alleges that the accused and others participated in a joint criminal enterprise aimed at permanent removal of Serbs from Krajina by the commission of crimes, or, in the course of which it was natural and foreseeable, that crimes would be committed. The indictment further charges the accused with otherwise committing, planning, instigating, ordering, and/or aiding and abetting the crimes charged. Finally, the indictment charges the accused with superior responsibility for criminal acts and/or omissions of their subordinates by failure to prevent the crimes or to punish the perpetrators thereof. In its legal characterizations, the Chamber adopts and applies the Tribunal's consistent case law with respect to the definition of these elements of the crimes and modes of liability charged in this case. In this decision, the Chamber will address the law more specifically only, when, in view of the submissions of the parties, this is required to explain the Chamber's findings. The volume of evidence before the Chamber and the character of the Rule 98 bis proceedings do not allow for a comprehensive discussion of the evidence in this decision. The Chamber did, however, consider the evidence in its entirety. The specific evidence that the Chamber will refer to in this decision is merely a selection of what the Chamber considered. In relation to the crimes charged, the Chamber verified whether the evidence addressed all the elements of each of the crimes. Similarly, the Chamber verified whether the evidence addressed all the requirements for criminal responsibility as charged for each accused. Finally, the Chamber verified whether the evidence, taken at its highest for the Prosecution, could lead a reasonable trier of fact to conclude, beyond a reasonable doubt, both that a crime has occurred, and that the accused are criminally responsible for it. All factual findings that follow are made using the evidentiary standard for Rule 98 bis decisions and do not prejudice any determinations to be made by the Chamber in its final written judgement. The Chamber will first examine the crime base, as alleged in Counts 1 through 9, and determine whether there is sufficient evidence with regard to each of the elements of the crimes to conclude that the counts should stand. The Chamber will next turn to the question of the individual criminal responsibility of the three accused. The Chamber initially turns to general elements and jurisdictional requirements that have to be proven under Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal. There is evidence of a major military operation in Krajina. Operation Storm, starting around 5.00 in the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, and involving combat between Croatian forces and forces of the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina. The case law of the Tribunal sets out that an armed conflict exists, and I quote: "Until a general conclusion of peace is reached; or, in the case of internal conflicts, a peaceful settlement is achieved." Noting the absence of evidence with respect to reaching any general conclusion of peace or achieving any peaceful settlement during the indictment period, the Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence to establish that an armed conflict commenced no later than at 5.00 a.m. on the 4th of August, 1995, and that it continued throughout the indictment period and extended throughout the geographic area covered by the indictment. With regard to the element of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population, the Gotovina Defence focussed, in its submissions, on the artillery attacks during Operation Storm. However, the indictment adopts a broader approach to this issue, setting out that all crimes charged occurred as part of a widespread or systematic attack against the Serb civilian population of the southern Krajina. The Chamber has received evidence of numerous incidents of persons taking possession from, and burning, houses in many villages during this period. Philip Berikoff, for example, travelled extensively through Krajina following Operation Storm and until the beginning of September 1995. He testified to having observed numerous burnt or burning houses, dead live stock, and burning fields in the area. He also testified to having observed groups of Croatian soldiers going from house to house in varies villages, taking items and livestock which they loaded onto trucks, after which the houses burst into flames. According to Berikoff, he observed on several indications, police directing traffic around these trucks and making markings on clipboards. His testimony indicates how visible the burning of houses and fields was from the roads on which he travelled. The following witnesses also testified about looting by members of the Croatian forces: Lennart Widen, about looting in Knin on the 6th of August, 1995; Herman Steenbergen, about looting in Gracac on the 6th of August, 1995, and during the subsequent weeks; Kari Anttila, about looting in Palanka, in Gracac municipality on the 18th of August, 1995; Witness 69, about looting in Zagrovic in Knin municipality around 11 August 1995; and Petar Colovic, about looting in Colovici in Orlic municipality a few days after the 5th of August, 1995. In examining the general elements of crimes against humanity, the Chamber also considered incidents of deportation, forcible transfer, murder, inhumane treatment, destruction, and plunder. Evidence relating to these crimes will be addressed shortly, when discussing each count of the indictment. The mentioned examples, as well as other evidence considered by the Chamber, indicate that the targets of the crimes were not merely a limited and randomly selected number of individuals. Rather, an examination of the number of incidents, the nature of those incidents, as well as the age and ethnicity of the persons subjected to crimes, provides a sufficient basis for establishing that there was an attack and that it was directed against the Serb civilian population of the southern portion of Krajina. The Chamber concludes that the evidence is sufficient to establish at this stage of the proceedings both that there was a widespread attack against the Serb civilian population of the southern portion of Krajina; and that the perpetrators must have known that their acts were part of that attack. The Chamber will now turn to examine the individual counts of the indictment. There is evidence of murder taking place during the indictment period and within the indictment area. For instance, Mile Djuric testified that on the 6th of August, 1995, in Plavno village in Knin municipality, soldiers detained and then threw his disabled father, Sava Djuric, into a burning workshop and locked the door. The Chamber received in evidence a death certificate for Sava Djuric. Additionally, the Chamber received evidence from Vesela Damjanic about the murder of her husband Lazo Damjanic on the 6th of August in Vrbnik in Orlic municipality. Vesela Damjanic stated that soldiers approached her house on that day and took her husband away. She heard the soldiers threaten her husband, and a short while later the witness heard shooting coming from the direction of where her husband had been taken. Lazo Damjanic did not return home, and on the 8th of August, the same two soldiers who had taken her husband away passed by her house and told Vesela Damjanic that she would not see her husband alive again. Relatives of the witness left the house to search for the body of Lazo Damjanic and informed the witness when they returned that they had found it. The Chamber also heard evidence about murders in Grubori hamlet in Plavno village in Knin municipality on the 25th of August, 1995. Jovan Grubor testified that on the morning of that day he saw three groups of soldiers in camouflage uniform walking on the asphalt road in the direction of Grubori and that later, when he arrived Grubori many houses were burning. He also testified that he saw the body of Jovo Grubor whose throat had been slit and whose body had been repeatedly stabbed. He further testified that he observed the bodies of Milica Grubor, Djuro Karanovic, and Milos Grubor, and in addition there are testimonies as well as there is documentary evidence indicating that these incidents were carried out by the Lucko Unit of the creation special police during a mopping up operation, in follow-up to the Operation Storm. In this respect, the Chamber refers in particular to the testimonies of Josip Celic, Zdravko Janic, and Josip Turkalj. This evidence addresses all the elements of murder as well as the requirements that the victims were not actively participating in hostilities at the time the offences were committed and that the murders were closely related to the armed conflict. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of murder for Counts 6 and 7 to stand. As mentioned, the Chamber will later turn to the question of whether any or all of the accused are individually criminally responsible for the crime of murder. There is evidence of the commission of inhumane acts and cruel treatment in the wake of Operation Storm. For instance, Bogdan Brkic stated that, sometime between Operation Storm and the 12th of August, 1995 armed and uniformed Croatian soldiers tied him to a tree in Palanka in Gracac municipality. They then placed a suit under his feet and set it on fire. In pain, he managed to kick it away. The soldiers also told him that they had killed his neighbour. Another example came from Draginja Urukalo, a woman aged 73 at the time, who stated that Croatian soldiers came to her village one day early in August 1995. After smashing some of her belongings, shooting at her house, and calling her a "Chetnik whore," the soldiers forced her to strip to her underwear and play basketball with her elderly neighbour. The Chamber also received evidence from Vesela Damjanic who testified that around the 16th of August, 1995, she saw three soldiers shouting at Djurdija Amanovic an elderly lady with mobility problems. The soldiers were also arguing about whether they should set her on fire. After the soldiers had left, Djurdija Amanovic told Vesela Damjanic that the soldiers had indeed tried to burn her and had accused her sons of being Chetniks. This evidence addresses all the elements of inhumane acts and cruel treatment as well as the requirements that the victims were not actively participating in hostilities at the time the offences were committed and that these acts were closely related to the armed conflict. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of inhumane acts and cruel treatment for Counts 8 and 9 to stand. There is evidence of plunder occurring during the indictment period and in the indictment area. The Chamber has already referred to some of this evidence earlier in its discussion of the general elements of crimes against humanity. For instance, Lennart Widen testified that in Knin, on the 6th of August, 1995, he observed many ransacked shops an apartments, soldiers of the creation Puma Brigade and civilian police carrying items, such as television sets, video recorders, and furniture, as well as military vehicles loaded with similar items departing from Knin. The evidence addresses all the elements of plunder as well as the requirements that the plunder had grave consequences for the victims and that it was closely related to the armed conflict. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of plunder for Count 4 to stand. The Chamber has also received evidence of large-scale destruction of houses or entire villages within the indictment period and area. For instance, several witnesses testified that on the 25th of August, 1995, numerous houses were set on fire and livestock killed in the hamlet of Grubori in Plavno village, in Knin municipality. The Chamber has also received video evidence, for example, P874, illustrating the destruction in the hamlet. As indicated earlier, there are witness testimonies as well as documentary evidence indicating that these actions were carried out by the Lucko Unit of the Croatian special police. A number of witnesses working for international organisations also testified about large-scale destruction of property that they had observed throughout the indictment area. For example Laila Malm, Philip Berikoff, and Alun Roberts testified about the extensive burning of houses in various villages in Kistanje municipality. The evidence indicates that at least some of these acts were carried out by Croatian soldiers. P707 and P709 contain pictures of the destruction in Knin, Kistanje, and Gracac. P754, P756, and P757 are videos showing the large-scale destruction of Kistanje and other villages in the area. Another example is the UNTV video footage in evidence under P26. Normand Boucher testified that he saw soldiers taking out jerrycans from a truck and taking them towards houses in the villages of Kosovo on the Knin-Drnis road. When Boucher returned some hours later, the houses and the adjacent crops were on fire. The evidence addresses all the elements of the war crime of wanton destruction and the requirement that these actions were closely related to the armed conflict. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of destruction for Count 5 to stand. There is evidence of deportation and forceable transfer of Serbs out of the Krajina in the indictment period. For instance, Marija Vecerina, a Serb woman, testified to a series of events which began on the 5th of August, 1995, and which eventually led her and some of her family members to leave Krajina for Serbia on the 16th of September, 1995. These circumstances included their being detained at various locations in Knin and Zadar from the 6th of August to the 16th of September, 1995, and their being subjected to other forms of coercive and intimidating treatment by Croatian soldiers and by Croatian civilian police. Mira Grubor testified that on the 5th of August, 1995, when Croatian forces entered town, she fled to the UN compound in Knin and that she remained there until the 16th of September, 1995, when she and others were transported in buses to Serbia. Before they could board the buses and leave the compound, however, people, Mira Grubor thought of as responsible to the Croatian authorities required them to sign a document stating that they had been treated in a humane way and that they voluntarily wished to move from Croatia to Serbia. Another Serb woman, Witness 3, testified about her experiences which were similar to those of Mira Grubor. She stated that she stayed at the UN compound in Knin for 40 days, starting on the 6th of August, and that a few days before the 16th of September, 1995, unknown persons told her that she had to sign a form stating that she was leaving Croatia voluntarily in order to be allowed to leave the UN compound. She signed the form to be allowed to leave the camp, but testified that she was not leaving Croatia voluntarily. The Chamber received such forms into evidence under P55 and P57. Witness 3 left the UN compound in a convoy of buses in the early morning hours of the 16th of September 1995 and arrived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia the day after. Other witnesses, including Mirko Ognjenovic, also testified about leaving Croatia from the UN compound in the convoy of buses in mid-September 1995. A report of the United Nations Secretary-General of the 23rd of August, 1995, in evidence as D90, states that theres with a mass exodus of the Krajina Serb population which create a humanitarian crisis with only 3.500 Serbs remaining in the former Sector North, and 2.000 Serbs remaining in the former Sector South, representing only a small percentage of the former Krajina Serb population. The evidence addresses all the elements of the crimes against humanity of deportation and inhumane acts consisting of forcible transfer. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of these crimes for Counts 2 and 3 to stand. The previously discussed crimes also constitute some of the underlying acts of the crime of persecution alleged in Count 1 of the indictment. There is evidence indicating that some of these acts were carried out as part of the crime of persecution against Krajina Serbs. For instance, Smiljana Mirkovic stated that on the 12th of August, 1995, in Polaca in Knin municipality, a soldier shot and killed Djurdija Mirkovic while cursing their Serbian mothers. Similar discriminatory statements were made by the perpetrators of other crimes on which the Chamber has received evidence. Petar Colovic stated that Croatian soldiers entered his village in Orlic municipality a few days after the 5th of August, 1995. The soldiers took personal belongs and livestock from the witness, and one of the soldiers also cursed the witness's mother and called her a Chetnik. Mira Grubor testified that while she was in the UN compound between the of 5th August and the 16th of September, 1995, she heard Croatian soldiers outside screaming things like "come out Chetnik bitches" and other similar pejorative statements. With regard to destruction of property and looting, the Chamber notes the evidence it received from Philip Berikoff, Peter Marti, Stig Marker Hansen, and through documents such as UNCIVPOL memo in evidence under P228, indicating that houses in Knin and elsewhere were marked as Croatian. There is evidence to the effect that the aim of this was to save these houses, unlike the non-Croat houses, from destruction or looting, although this was not always successful. The evidence addresses all of the elements of the crimes against humanity of persecution. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence of persecution for Count 1 to stand. Although the Gotovina Defence considered that Count 1 should be dismissed in its entirety, it also invited the Chamber, in the alternative, to dismiss Count 1 in part, namely with regard to the underlying act of unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects. As mentioned earlier, Rule 98 bis, as amended in December 2004 provides for a review of the evidence on a count-by-count basis and not with regard to specific charges of the. Since the Chamber considers that the evidence presented is sufficient for at least some of the underlying acts of persecution, Count 1 will stand in its entirety. The Chamber does not accept the Gotovina Defence's suggested approaches to dismissing counts in part. Having found a sufficient evidentiary basis, under the aforementioned Rule 98 bis standard of review of evidence, for the crimes charged in each and all counts of indictment, the Chamber now turns to the responsibility of the accused for those crimes. The Chamber will first examine the evidence with regard to the mode of liability of participation in a joint criminal enterprise. As set out in the case law of the Tribunal, the elements of this mode of liability are: A plurality of persons; a common objective which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute; and the participation of the accused in the objective's implementation. The contribution of an accused need not have been substantial or necessary to the achievement of the common objective. However, it should at least be a significant contribution to the crimes forming part of the common objective. The mens rea required is that the participants in the joint criminal enterprise, including the accused, had a common state of mind, namely, the state of mind that the statutory crimes - I should say crime or crimes - through which the common objective were to be achieved, should be carried out. This is what in the case law is referred to as the first form of joint criminal enterprise, and the Prosecution has charged all three accused with this mode of liability with regard to Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment. The Prosecution has also charged the accused, in addition or in the alternative, with the third form of joint criminal enterprise. The mens rea required with respect to this charge is that the resulting crime or crimes were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise, and that the accused was aware of this and participated with that awareness. There is evidence of a joint criminal enterprise between the accused, with the objective of the permanent removal of Serbs from Krajina. When examining the first two elements of this mode of liability, the Chamber considered evidence addressing the alleged participants in the joint criminal enterprise agreeing, conspiring, discussing, or otherwise manifesting the existence of a common objective, which amounts to or involves the commission of crimes provided for in the Statute. The Chamber also examined the evidence on the commission of such crimes in the indictment area and during the indictment period. The Chamber finally considered whether this evidence allows, on its own or together with the other evidence, for an inference as to the existence of a common objective. The Chamber received into evidence the audio-recording and minutes of a meeting held between President Tudjman, Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Markac, and others at Brioni on the 31st of July, 1995. In this respect, the Chamber considered Exhibit P461 and the submissions made by the Gotovina Defence on the 1st of April, 2009, with regard to the transcription and translation of the recordings of this meeting. During the meeting, the participants discussed, among other things, that civilians would be leaving the area in connection with the armed operation. President Tudjman stated, for example, that: "It is important that those civilians set out, and then the army will follow them, and when the column sets out, they will have a psychological impact on each other." And Mr. Gotovina then responded: "A large number of civilians are already evacuating Knin and heading towards Banja Luka and Belgrade. That means that if we continue this pressure, probably for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians, just those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving." The participants further discussed the possible routes that should be left open for the civilians to leave Croatia. It was also agreed at the meeting that information should be spread amongst the Serb civilian population that Serb civilians were already leaving the area. In proposing a text for a leaflet or a radio or television message, President Tudjman stated: "Serbs, you are already withdrawing, and so forth, and we are appealing to you not to withdraw. We guarantee ... this means giving them a way out." This literally quote was followed by words strongly implying that civil rights would ostensibly be guaranteed. The Chamber has also heard witness's testimonies with regard to the objective of the permanent removal of Serbs from Krajina. Peter Galbraith testified that President Tudjman had informed him after Krajina Serbs had left Croatia in August 1995 that those Serbs who had left could not return to Croatia. Galbraith also testified about the laws on confiscation of property which required those who had left Croatia to return within a short period of time or risk losing their property. Galbraith further testified that although this time-limit was eventually abandoned, this was only after intense international pressure on Croatia. From his contacts with President Tudjman, and others in the Croatian political leadership, Galbraith formed the opinion that the mentioned laws as well as other measures, including systematic looting and burning of Serb homes, were all aimed at preventing those Serbs who had left from ever returning. The Chamber has already made findings on the various counts in the indictment under the Rule 98 bis standard of review. As described, there is evidence showing that many crimes were committed throughout the indictment period by Croatian soldiers or special police on the ground in Krajina. In particular, the Chamber found that the evidence is sufficient to conclude that there was a widespread attack against the Serb civilian population of the southern portion of Krajina. The Chamber concludes that, for the purposes of a review of the evidence, pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules, there is sufficient evidence of the existence of a common objective aimed at the permanent removal of Serbs from Krajina by force or threat of force, persecution, forced transfer, and deportation, as well as appropriation and destruction of property as charged in Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment. The Chamber further concludes that there is sufficient evidence that the crimes charged in the Counts 6 through 9 were natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of this common objective. The Chamber will next turn to the third element of joint criminal enterprise; namely, the participation of the accused in the objective's implementation. Both Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac participated in the aforementioned Brioni meeting during which participants discussed how civilians would leave Krajina. There is also evidence indicating that Mr. Gotovina was in command and control of Croatian forces within the Split Military District and that Mr. Markac was in command of special police operations in Sector South during and after Operation Storm. As indicated earlier, there is evidence that at least some of the crimes under each of the Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment were committed by Croatian forces, including the special police. The Chamber also received further evidence placing Mr. Gotovina, Mr. Markac on the ground in Krajina and being involved in military or special police operations during the indictment period. In this respect, there is both documentary evidence and testimony implicating Mr. Markac in activities attempting to obscure crimes committed by the Lucko Unit of the special police in Grubori on the 25th of August, 1995. The Chamber refers in particular to the testimonies of Zdravko Janic and Josip Celic. The Chamber has also received evidence of Mr. Gotovina's awareness of crimes committed by men under his command during and following Operation Storm. For example, in a letter to Mr. Gotovina on the 5th of August, 1995, Alain Forand expressed concerns about significant looting and destruction occurring in Knin. This letter is in evidence under P347. On the 12th of August, 1995, HV assistant commander for political affairs, Captain Mario Tomasovic, addressed a notification entitled "Warning" to, amongst others, Mr. Gotovina. It noted that the success of Operation Storm had been partly brought into question by the inappropriate acts of individual Croatian soldiers and stressed the need to prevent the continued destruction and looting of property, killing of livestock, and inappropriate conduct towards civilians and prisoners of war. This notification is in evidence as P918. In a letter dated the 13th of September, 1995, and in evidence as Exhibit P407, Mr. Gotovina wrote to General Cervenko, noting that Alun Roberts had stated that: "The Croatian army is burning, looting, and violating human rights." Mr. Gotovina further indicated that he did not believe that this conduct or that of his men conflicted with Croatian state policy. The evidence heard allows for the conclusion that Mr. Gotovina had the power and ability to discipline soldiers under his command. However, the Chamber heard evidence from expert witness Reynaud Theunens that Mr. Gotovina primarily used his powers to discipline men for violations or crimes that would jeopardize the accomplishment of specific combat tasks and combat operations, rather than for crimes against the civilian population such as looting and burning. The Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence to establish the participation of Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac in the joint criminal enterprise as described, and that their participation amounted to a significant contribution to crimes charged in Counts 1 through 5. The Chamber further concludes that the aforementioned evidence is sufficient to establish both that Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac intended the commission of these crimes and that they knowingly took the risk that the other crimes charged in the indictment would be committed as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the implementation of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Regard to Mr. Cermak, there is evidence that on the 5th of August, 1995, President Tudjman personally appointed him commander of the Knin garrison, with the stated tasks of restoring normal life in and around Knin and dealing with the media and representatives of the international community. Mr. Markac remained in his position throughout the indictment period. Witness 86 and Stjepan Buhin testified that Mr. Cermak chaired meetings held almost daily at his office in Knin, in which representatives from various civilian and military structures, including the civilian police, participated. During these meetings, Mr. Cermak was informed, among other things, about crimes occurring in and around Knin. There is evidence of cooperation between Mr. Cermak and the other two accused; for instance, with regard to freedom of movement and special police mopping up operations. Mr. Cermak issued documents allowing or denying free movement of civilians or members of international organisations. His work also included administering a sanitary team disposing of dead bodies and livestock. There is evidence that Mr. Cermak, at times, either denied that members of Croatian forces had committed crimes, attempted to downplay these crimes, or promised that investigations would take place, but such investigations either were not carried out or were not conducted until much later. After the killings carried out this Grubori on 25th of August, 1995, there is evidence indicating that Mr. Cermak knew that civilians had been killed and that houses in the hamlet had been burned down by members of the special police. For example, on the 26th of August, Richard Lyntton interviewed Mr. Cermak and informed him about the killing of two elderly men in the hamlet. Mr. Cermak also visited Grubori himself around the same time, and observed the destruction of houses. Nevertheless, through various communications during the subsequent days, including those in evidence as P603 and P1222, Mr. Cermak relayed to members of international organisations the version of events given to him by the special police, despite evidence indicating that he knew that this version was not reliable. The Chamber also received evidence of Mr. Cermak's personal involvement in securing the departure of hundreds of Serb civilians from the UN compound in Knin on busses to Serbia. The Chamber earlier referred to Witness 3 and Mira Grubor who each in various ways had been forced to leave their homes and subsequently came to the UN compound. The Chamber received from Alain Forand and other witnesses evidence according to which Mr. Cermak had a central role in the negotiations between Croatia and the United Nations regarding the fate of the Serb displaced persons at the UN compound. Moreover, the Chamber received documentary evidence, under Exhibit D316, that portrayed Mr. Cermak as one of the key persons responsible for the operation to move to Serbia the Serb displaced civilians in a convoy of 35 buses on the 16th and 17th of September, 1995. Taking the evidence at its highest for the Prosecution, the Chamber concludes that there is sufficient evidence to establish the participation of Mr. Cermak in the joint criminal enterprise, alongside the two other accused, and that his participation amounted to a significant contribution to the crimes charged in Counts 1 through 5. The Chamber further concludes that the evidence is sufficient to show that Mr. Cermak intended the commission of these crimes, and knowingly took the risk that the other crimes charged in the indictment would be committed as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the implementation of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Having thus found, under the Rule 98 bis standard of review, sufficient evidence to sustain all counts of the indictment for each of the accused under one mode of liability, the Chamber does not, at present, need to examine the other modes of liability alleged in the indictment. In conclusion, all three accused have a case to answer on all nine counts of the indictment. I continue with a related, although a bit separate issue. On the 23rd of March, 2009, the Prosecution referred to a list of 32 specific murder victims mentioned in the indictment, as well as the original and further clarification. The Prosecution conceded that for these victims it had not presented any evidence of murder. This can be found at transcript page 17.415. And on the 27th of March, the Prosecution filed this list. I am now addressing the Defence. The crimes for which -- I would say especially the Gotovina Defence, argued that no evidence had been presented was far longer than 32 names or persons identified. The Chamber notes that five out of the list of 32 of the Prosecution's list do not appear in the, by far, longer list of the Defence. The Chamber wonders whether the Defence disagrees on those specific five, that no evidence has been presented, or whether it agrees with the Prosecution that no evidence has been presented. And I just give these five, the first one being scheduled killing 83, Saric Danica, that's number 1 on the Prosecution list. Number 26 on the Prosecution's list, killing number 234, Supeljak Mirko. Number 27 on the Prosecutor's list, killing number 239, Pribojan Darinka. Number 28 on the Prosecution's list, killing number 243, Miljevic Ilija. And number 29 on the Prosecutor's list, killing number 270, Simic Milica. The Chamber would like to establish whether or not the Defence would agree on no evidence having been presented, in relation to these five cases, because the Prosecution states that no evidence was presented but the Defence has not listed these five persons as cases where no evidence was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would -- in all honesty have to look at our records on it, but can I tell you right now that if the Prosecution believes it hasn't proven a charge, I'm not going to dispute it. So -- we will certainly go back and look at it ourselves. Obviously I don't think that our list was intended to be exhaustive when we recited it at the 98 bis hearing, and therefore it is certainly possible that there are more names than the ones we listed. But those were the names in light of the amount of time to prepare on the variety of issues we were addressing that we came up with at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the other Defence teams. What their position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can't add anything to what Mr. Misetic has said, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Same position, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that, although still subject to verification, that there seems to be, in principle, agreement among the parties, and the Chamber takes note of that. That no evidence of murder has been presented with regard to all of the 32 victims mentioned in the Prosecution's notification of the 27th of March. And, Mr. Misetic, I asked only about the five, but I took it from your submissions under 98 bis that the remaining 27, that there was agreement already on those. If the verification would lead the Prosecution -- the Defence teams to any other conclusion, the Chamber would like to be informed so as to be able to correct what is now noted and put on the record as an agreement among the parties, in relation to the 32 victims. This concludes the Chamber decisions and the related issue, under Rule 98 bis. As I said before, I have a few matters. The first we can deal with in open session. It is a notification of the lifting of confidentiality of the Prosecution's motion seeking the production of documents obtained by the Gotovina Defence and the fact that it has been denied in a confidential decision. I read it in its entirety. The Chamber informs the public that on the 22nd of January, 2009, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion in which it requested the Chamber, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, to order the Gotovina Defence to produce any documents in its possession obtained from sources other than the Prosecution, that fall within the Prosecution's Artillery Document Request made to Croatia. In a confidential decision to be filed this afternoon, or later this morning, the Chamber denied that motion and also lifted the confidential status of the motion and its Appendix C. Appendices A and B to the motion and the Chamber's decision are to remain confidential, in order to avoid any risk of inference with pending Rule 54 bis matters in this case. And this concludes the statement of the Chamber in this respect. The next -- for the next item I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The last item on my agenda is that the Gotovina Defence asked to make further submissions on the issue of the lifting of restriction on communication in relation to a witness which may be re-called. And I -- of course, I do not know exactly what are you going to say. I think until now, it was -- I don't think that there is anything confidential in the issue itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We discussed that in public session on the 6th of March, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I see you're not jumping, but you're raising your eyebrows, which is also up for direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour, for attending to our possible concerns. Just wondering about the extent to which submissions related to an issue of contact can -- or communication can take the inadvertent form of communication. And since I don't know what the submissions might be, it raises that potential concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said earlier when I said I don't know what the content of Mr. Misetic's observations will be. But I think he gave it some thought and considers that where the matter was raised publicly earlier, that he certainly has thought about whether his submissions would create any need to change the status of this discussion. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just have one moment, Mr. President. Just as a matter of the status, it's my recollection that not only did we discuss it in public, but the Chamber's filing on Friday filing the e-mails was done publicly, and if I'm not mistaken, the Prosecution filed their submission publicly, so I don't see why our reply would suddenly have to be confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not knowing what you're going to say, of course, Mr. Tieger says that if you talk about non-communication, then submissions in itself could be a form of communication. But you are aware of that, and that I take it that you have sufficiently considered that, so you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Briefly there were two main issues that I wanted to address in the Prosecution's response. First of all, the reason that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reason that we need to conduct this witness, obviously, he is an important witness with respect to artillery issues in this case. Information continues to come in at a pretty significant clip. We have to prepare witnesses not the least of which are expert witnesses on artillery issues, and we are hindered by an inability to contact an important witness about a wide variety of issues including to check additional information that was disclosed to us last week by an order of the Chamber. We had no objection initially to the non-contact because it was our assumption that if he were recalled, it would be recalled while Prosecution's case was still open. That obviously hasn't happened, and we've now completed the 98 bis stage. We at this point have no instruction from the Chamber as to whether there is any intent, and if so, when to call him back, and so we're hampered in our preparations, and I can use an example. Mr. Theunens testified here. I'm -- I feel reasonably confident that once he finished testifying, the Prosecution didn't stop communicating with him. As a matter of fact, I'm pretty sure they now -- I would suggest regularly contact him regarding issues in this case. Similarly the fact that Mr. Rajcic completed testimony does not change the fact that he is still a valuable source of information for the Defence in preparing its case whether he ultimately comes to testify or not. With respect to why we sent an e-mail, my understanding of the procedural history of this is the Prosecution did not file a formal motion but sent a request to the Chamber in the form of an e-mail. The Chamber responded with an instruction in the form of an e-mail, and therefore we also sent an e-mail. The fact that they had an opportunity the next day because we happened to be sitting in court to raise the issue is in our view certainly fine, I have no objection to it, but at the time we sent our request, we of course did not have court the next day, but we could raise the matter earlier with the Chamber. And in light of the timing issues, we also, frankly, fell that we can't afford 14 days response plus reply because the time for us to prepare our Defence is running. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as e-mail communications are concerned, there certainly was an urgency in the matter, that is also a reason why the Chamber has chosen to respond by e-mail. At the same time, by putting all these e-mails on the record, the Chamber did stick to its tripartition, purely practical matters can be exchanged by e-mail. If not purely practical if there is any e-mail exchange, it should be put on the record sooner or later. If it is a matter of substance, then the e-mails should be filed so as to make the record fully transparent. In this case, finally, the Chamber was in a position at this moment to -- because we had to file something anyhow to use that opportunity to do what we expect the parties to do under those circumstances. At this moment I think that if everyone is fully and constantly aware of what the background thoughts are, then there should be no reason for major disagreement or major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just -- I forgot to add one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there were two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I had two things, but there is a third matter I should have addressed initially. We are going to add Mr. Rajcic to our Defence witness list as well. The reason being that there may be issues that come up with witnesses in the Defence case concerning artillery where new factual matters come up that will -- or new documents come in from the Prosecution or the Defence that need further comment by Mr. Rajcic. For that reason when we disclose our witness list, he will be on the witness list. To that extent, I just wanted the Chamber to know that in its consideration of how we recall Mr. Rajcic, whether we wait to see if, at the end of the day, towards the end of the Defence case, he will be recalled again, and therefore potentially a third time, or if for whatever reason we ultimately chose not to recall him because there weren't additional issues, there is of course - we're in the Defence case now essentially - the opportunity for the Chamber then to give the Prosecution an opportunity to recall him because of the Defence has chosen not to call him, even though he is on the witness list. But at this point we cannot know for sure, and it depends really on what happens in the initial parts of the Defence case whether the Defence will be calling Mr. Rajcic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, that is it clearly on the record now. These are the matters that the Chamber wanted to raise. Are there any other matters that we have to urgently deal with? Because we'll not be in court for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour, again, without making a drama out it as the Court has urged, I just want to underscore the Prosecution's earlier expressed concern about the distinction between e-mails and motions. I understand that at the both ends of the spectrum, formal motion on the one hand, practical communications on the other that are e-mails, the Court' guidance that when something that normally would fall at the practical end of the spectrum, may stray into something substantive that needs to be memorialised in a formal pleading, it does so. But that should not slip into the supplanting of e-mails for formal motions, and we've expressed our concern about that; we continue to have that concern for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear we have to find a fair balance between practicality and transparency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just comment. I agree with that, just in the context of this particular motion, from our perspective, we wish to be treated the same way. And again as I say there was no formal order from the Chamber that had been filed in the first place. But certainly, if e-mails being filed is something that the Chamber wishes, and I have no problem with that, we can file them, but again our issue was with respect to the urgency that the matter needed to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties might receive soon further message from the Chamber staff on what to copy the Chamber and on what not to copy the Chamber. That is a matter which was discussed recently with the Chamber and the Chamber staff. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing more to be discussed at this moment. The Chamber will adjourn until the 27th of May, when a pre-Defence conversation will be held. The courtroom in which this conference will be held is not yet known, so the parties are invited to inquire into which courtroom we expect you to appear. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of May, 2009.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.38 a.m.,
